title: Salem Advocate Earns Rare Federal Credential to Defend Immigrants in Court
excerpt: Jessica Jennings of Lutheran Community Services Northwest is the organization's first fully accredited representative — one of just 11 in Oregon — a credential that lets her take asylum and deportation cases before immigration judges.
body:
• Jessica Jennings, an advocate with Lutheran Community Services Northwest's Safe Route Immigration Program in Salem, has earned full accreditation from the U.S. Department of Justice — the organization's first fully accredited representative.
  • Full accreditation allows a non-lawyer to represent clients before immigration courts and the Board of Immigration Appeals, not just U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
  • Oregon has only 11 fully accredited representatives, according to a Justice Department report updated Sept. 13 — seven of them at Portland's Innovation Law Lab.
  • The Salem office can now expand into asylum and deportation defense cases that previously required referral to an attorney.

A Salem immigration advocate can now stand beside her clients in immigration court — a rare federal credential in Oregon that turns a paperwork helper into a courtroom defender. Jessica Jennings, who works in Lutheran Community Services Northwest's Safe Route Immigration Program, has become the organization's first fully accredited representative through the U.S. Department of Justice, the Statesman Journal reported.

Until now, Jennings held partial accreditation, which limited her to representing clients before U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Full accreditation opens a second venue: the Executive Office for Immigration Review, which runs the immigration courts and the Board of Immigration Appeals. For the Salem office, that means it can now take on asylum and deportation defense cases directly instead of sending clients elsewhere to find a lawyer.

A year of training on top of a full caseload

Department of Justice accreditation authorizes non-lawyers to represent people in immigration legal matters, but only through recognized nonprofits that serve low-income and indigent clients. Jennings, an Oregonian since she was 13, spent the past year preparing for the upgrade while carrying her full-time caseload — shadowing attorneys in Portland, Vancouver and Seattle, and meeting regularly with a mentor attorney.

"With all the changes happening, I think we're all having to invest a lot of time in learning."

— Jessica Jennings, Safe Route Immigration Program

A scarce credential statewide

The numbers show how unusual the credential is. A Justice Department report updated Sept. 13 lists 14 recognized organizations in Oregon with accredited representatives, but only five have at least one who is fully accredited. Statewide, the report counts 11 fully accredited representatives — seven of them at Portland's Innovation Law Lab — leaving Salem and most of the rest of the state with almost no accredited courtroom representation.

Why it matters for immigrant families

For immigrants facing removal proceedings, having a qualified representative can determine the outcome of a case — and private immigration attorneys are often out of reach for low-income families. Nonprofit legal aid fills that gap, but representation inside immigration court has been the bottleneck. Jennings' upgrade means Salem-area clients can now get asylum and deportation defense from the same office that handled their initial applications. The timing is pointed: last week, a federal judge in Oregon questioned the credibility of ICE officials at a hearing on warrantless arrests in the state, the Statesman Journal reported — a sign of the enforcement pressure immigrant communities are under.

What's next

With full accreditation in hand, the Salem office can begin building out its deportation-defense caseload. Safe Route Immigration serves clients in Portland, Beaverton, McMinnville and Salem, as well as sites across Washington. For Jennings, the credential caps a year of extra training. For the immigrants who walk into the Salem office, it means the advocate across the desk can now follow their case all the way into court.
